analysis.one_liner: Froze credit card interest rates and fees on existing balances until new consumer protections took effect.
analysis.headline: The bill to freeze credit card rates before the new consumer rules took effect was introduced and placed on the Senate calendar but never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2009, Congress had already passed the CARD Act, a law adding new protections for credit card users, but its main rules were not scheduled to take effect until February 2010. In the months before that date, card companies were raising interest rates on balances people already owed. This bill would have banned those increases — on interest rates, fees, and finance charges on existing balances — from the day it was signed until the new law's protections kicked in. It never got a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Households carrying credit card debt — especially those already behind on balances during the recession — would have been protected from rate and fee increases on money they had already borrowed, for the months between enactment and the CARD Act's February 2010 effective date. Card issuers' practices of repricing existing balances ahead of the deadline would have been stopped during that window.

how_it_helps.text: It barred creditors from raising interest rates, fees, or finance charges on any existing credit card balance during the freeze period.
It also barred creditors from changing the repayment terms on outstanding balances, except for the narrow adjustments the CARD Act itself allowed.
It was designed to take effect immediately upon enactment, without waiting for regulations, so the protection could not be delayed.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks, which would have lost the ability to raise rates and fees on existing balances for roughly the final months before the CARD Act took effect. Critics warned the freeze could lead lenders to tighten credit or shift costs to new accounts; cardholders would not have paid the higher rates.

drawbacks.text: A blanket rate freeze applies to all card issuers regardless of their financial condition; lenders argued that being unable to reprice outstanding balances during a period of rising defaults would force them to tighten credit elsewhere or raise rates on new borrowing.

The freeze was a temporary patch covering only the months before the CARD Act's rules took effect; it did not address the underlying cost of card debt, and cardholders still owed the balances at their existing rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real and time-sensitive: millions of cardholders were facing rate increases on balances they had already borrowed, and the freeze would have stopped that for several months. The main cost is the standard objection to any price freeze: blocking lenders from repricing risk can lead them to tighten credit or raise rates on new accounts instead, and some issuers would have shifted costs to fees on new spending. Those tradeoffs, however, applied for only about four months, after which the CARD Act's own rules would take over, which is why supporters saw the freeze as a low-risk bridge rather than a permanent price control. The bigger design question is why a temporary bridge to existing law never received even a committee hearing or a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and placed directly on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but no one ever scheduled it for floor action, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd introduced the bill on October 26, 2009, and it was read and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar the next day.
Twenty-one Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors.
The bill's action history ends on October 27, 2009; it was never referred to committee, never marked up, and never scheduled for a floor vote during the remainder of the 111th Congress.
No vote was ever recorded on the bill, and it did not become law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: they retained the ability to raise rates and fees on balances cardholders already owed right up until the new CARD Act protections took effect in February 2010.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; Chairman, Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed freezing rates on existing balances, arguing it would restrict the availability of credit, in the run-up to the CARD Act's effective date.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the bill never reached a vote where the split could be measured.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill would have blocked issuers from raising rates and fees on balances already owed during the months before the CARD Act took effect, freezing revenue on a large stock of existing debt. Issuers had been repricing existing balances in anticipation of the new rules, so the freeze targeted exactly that practice.

Banking groups warned that a rate freeze would restrict lending during the recovery, since lenders could not reprice for risk on existing balances. The effect was limited to a several-month window on existing debt, after which the CARD Act's own rules governed.
